item.title: Republicans face a crowded agenda and little time before handing Congress to Democrats
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans on Capitol Hill are on the clock. They have less than two months left in power before the new, Democrat-led Congress is sworn in and their window of unified control in Washington, D.C., comes to an end. Even as the votes are still being counted, GOP leaders have been putting together plans for what they hope to accomplish before they lose power. "Our job is nowhere close to being finished yet," House Speaker Mike Johnson reportedly told attendees at a watch party Tuesday night as Democratic victories piled up. The period between the November election and the day in early January when new lawmakers are sworn in, often called the "lame duck" session, can be quite productive as lawmakers move with urgency to get things done while they still can. Some of the most important actions taken by Congress in modern history — the legislative response to the Watergate scandal, the Clinton impeachment, the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and several Supreme Court confirmations — all happened during various lame duck windows. Republicans will have a long list of priorities when Congress reconvenes on Monday, but there are also plenty of potential hurdles that could hinder their progress. Here's a look at what congressional Republicans want to do and some of the possible curveballs that could derail their plans. What needs to get done Congress will have two "must-pass" items on its agenda when it gets back to work next week: avoiding another government shutdown and passing an annual defense policy bill. Leaders from both parties say they want to get both bills done, but disagreement on the specifics could make for a bumpy and time-consuming process. The government will shut down again on Dec. 12 if Congress doesn't pass a funding bill to keep it open. After enduring the two longest shutdowns in history over the past two years, neither party appears eager to let another one happen. The big point of disagreement could be timing. Republican leaders are reportedly eyeing a bill that would lock in current spending levels for a full year, but Democrats have an incentive to advocate for a short-term bill that sets them up to enact their own spending priorities once they're in full control of Congress. Negotiations over the defense budget could be even thornier. The Trump administration has asked Congress for $1.5 trillion in military funding for 2027. Democrats have balked at that number, demanding that the price tag be reduced by hundreds of billions of dollars. Reports suggest that the administration may be open to shrinking its budget request, but landing on a final number that both parties and the president can agree on could prove challenging — particularly if the White House insists on including more funding for the war with Iran. "I don't know what [Trump's] going to want. I don't know how we're going to figure out the money. So no, I don't have easy answers to that," Rep. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, told Politico on Wednesday. Even if both bills eventually get passed, drawn-out negotiations could eat up precious time and leave little room for Congress to do much else before the end of the year. Republicans' 'Last Supper' In the wake of Tuesday's losses, some Republican lawmakers have begun advocating for their party to pass one last major budget bill jam-packed with GOP priorities. To do that, they'd need to use the same process they utilized to pass Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill, which creates a pathway to circumvent the Senate filibuster and approve legislation without any Democratic votes. "It's time to wake up and smell the coffee," Trump adviser Jason Miller told GOP lawmakers on Wednesday. "You have one job. Get everything on President Trump's agenda through in the limited days we have." Before the election, Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno told reporters that he would push for a "giant" spending package during the lame-duck session if the GOP lost both chambers of Congress. "It'll be the Last Supper," he said. Actually getting another Republican megabill passed could be a steep challenge. Negotiations over the massive list of complex provisions within the One Big Beautiful Bill took months and consumed big chunks of the congressional calendar. Republicans may also have a numbers problem. Any bill they put forward would need near-unanimous support within their party in both chambers. That includes outgoing senators Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, who have been at odds with the president in the late stages of their time in Congress. Republicans also have other, less ambitious priorities that could be at risk if they dedicate their time and energy to another huge party-line budget bill. One of those priorities is a bipartisan proposal to overhaul the permitting process for energy projects, which would make it easier to build both renewable and fossil fuel infrastructure. There's also a sweeping slate of reforms to college sports , a number of Trump-nominated judges awaiting confirmation , cryptocurrency legislation and more that could end up on the GOP's long to-do list. Potential curveballs One of the biggest questions looming over Washington, D.C., since Tuesday is whether any of the Supreme Court's conservative justices might retire during the lame-duck session. With Democrats pledging to prevent Trump from putting another "right-winger" on the court, this could be a conservative justice's last chance — potentially for years — to retire with the confidence that their replacement is likely to share their ideology. Neither of the court's two oldest justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, has given any indication that they're considering stepping down — in fact, Alito has reportedly been unequivocal about his plans to stay on the bench. But if one of them did, Republicans would be heavily incentivized to put everything else on the back burner to rush the confirmation of their replacement before Democrats gain the power to block Trump's nominees for the rest of his presidency. Republicans' calendar may also get scrambled by some of their own outgoing members. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has been a key voice behind the push for disclosures about the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein, has said he plans to force a second vote on the issue before he leaves Congress. Massie has said he's also planning to introduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced heavy scrutiny for his role in carrying out the war in Iran. Tillis recently told CBS News that Hegseth faces a "reckoning" when Congress reconvenes next week. It's unclear how much support Massie's impeachment effort has in the House, but even if it failed, it could consume valuable time Republican leaders would rather spend on other priorities. The same would be true of confirmation hearings for a new defense secretary if reports that Trump is considering firing Hegseth prove to be accurate. item.title: Judge halts construction on Trump’s arch — right after a federal panel approved it
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from beginning construction on President Trump's proposed triumphal arch late Thursday, siding — for now — with a group of Vietnam veterans and the District of Columbia and Virginia, which sued to stop the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that the government cannot start any "construction-related activity" for 14 days, while further legal proceedings play out. In a 33-page ruling , Chutkan wrote that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing the federal government did not follow required legal processes before moving to build the 250-foot triumphal arch. She also said Virginia and D.C. likely have standing to sue, pointing to "tangible economic harms" caused by traffic problems at the construction site. The ruling came shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission voted Thursday night to approve plans for the arch, giving the final go-ahead for the monument that's set to be constructed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The White House praised the commission's approval of the arch, but criticized Chutkan's order temporarily blocking construction. "We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch — a tribute to 250 years of American greatness," Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said in a statement. The NCPC, which acts as the federal government's planning agency for the region and is stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 to greenlight the project after almost 9 hours of public comments from members of Congress, veterans, architects and Washington, D.C., and Virginia residents. Chutkan's order aside, it's unclear how soon construction of the arch could start, though the Justice Department said in a court filing last month that it could begin as soon as Thursday. In a separate filing Wednesday night, the Trump administration said that a construction company "may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval" at the site. Ahead of the meeting, the NCPC's executive director, Mark Paoletta, recommended approval of the final site and building plans for the structure, which is supposed to celebrate 250 years of American independence. Paoletta, the top lawyer at the Office of Management and Budget, heralded Mr. Trump's "historic vision" for the structure and said it would be the "grandest arch ever built by mankind." But California Rep. Jared Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, said during the hearing that the arch is "illegal" and would "disrupt the solemn connection" between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. "This arch would dishonor America, our ideals, and our laws," Huffman said during remarks to the planning commission, adding that Congress is the appropriate body for debating the proposed monument. One Marine veteran who spoke in opposition to the proposal, Jimi Shaughnessy, said "a dominating arch with a carnival-like atmosphere of tourists, food trucks and buses is abhorrent and insulting to those who gave all and to their families." "Instead of focusing on the issues facing military families, this administration is intent on spending taxpayer dollars to site, plan, and design a monument no one asked for, and are content with bypassing any laws or regulations that may prevent them from breaking ground," he said. The arch itself will be 166 feet tall and topped with "three gilded figures" — a gold, winged female figure flanked by a gold flying eagle on each side — bringing its overall height to 250 feet, according to documents filed with the NCPC. The structure will sit close to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, though the Federal Aviation Administration determined it will pose "no hazard to air navigation," with a "condition for safety lighting that includes a non-standard eternal flame and continuous floodlighting." The arch will also feature an observation deck, and the Trump administration has estimated that it could draw between 2,000 and 22,400 visitors each day. It's expected to take three years to build the arch, which will be located in the center of what is called Memorial Circle, across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial. It's unclear how much the project will cost, and who will foot the bill. Mr. Trump said in September that his "Triumphal Arch" would be a "top grade Military Complex" and house drones and sniper ammunition. But the documents from the NCPC do not include the military usage. Lawyers for the Justice Department declined to provide more details about the national security features in an October hearing. The commission received more than 1,300 public comments about the project, most of which were in opposition, it said. The NCPC's approval came as Chutkan weighed how to act. The group of Vietnam War veterans, as well as the Commonwealth of Virginia and the city of Washington, D.C., have filed lawsuits arguing that the Trump administration is acting without congressional authorization and is not complying with the required procedures to construct the monument. In an order Tuesday, Chutkan required the government to provide her notice within one hour of any NCPC vote and a thirty-minute notice to any preparation for construction of the arch to give her time to issue a decision on whether to block construction. The government filed the required notices late Thursday, and Chutkan responded by issuing the temporary restraining order that blocked "construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at the site. In a hearing last month, Chutkan said the most important issue for her is whether the Vietnam War veterans had the legal right to sue. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court found that a group of plaintiffs who brought a similar suit to block the White House ballroom construction likely did not have legal standing to challenge the project. In court filings, the Justice Department called the plaintiffs' motions "breathless" and urged Chutkan to follow the Supreme Court's decision in the White House ballroom case, but attorneys for the groups of plaintiffs argued that their legal arguments were different than the ballroom case and urged Chutkan to halt the arch's construction. Two of the plaintiffs, Vietnam veterans Michael Lemmon and Shaun Byrnes, told Chutkan in a hearing last month that the arch construction would impact their experience when visiting graves at Arlington National Cemetery, and said they would be harmed by the arch's size and purpose. In a separate suit brought in late October, Virginia and the District of Columbia sued, and the case was assigned to Chutkan, who had heard arguments the day before from the Vietnam veterans group. The state's attorneys general argued that "as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm" on them because "the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-arch-approval-national-capital-planning-commission/

item.title: Vance faces a 2028 dilemma as Republicans question his ties to Trump
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP's devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing criticism for blaming the losses on the Iran war and other big-name Republicans appearing to stake out their own positions. The losses have created a huge opening for GOP White House hopefuls, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), to go against Vance. It’s a fact seemingly recognized by Vance, who was quick to blame the Iran war for the historic drubbings, and Republicans at large. “The election results were bad news for every leader across the party, given the scale of the losses, but they were particularly tough for Vance’s 2028 prospects,” said Kevin Madden, the veteran Republican strategist who served as a senior adviser on Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign. “Vance is now in the position of serving as a loyal vice president to a lame-duck president whose approval rating is in the 30’s and whose influence on the future of the party could be in question,” Madden added. Vance has long been seen as the front-runner to succeed President Trump as the GOP standard-bearer. A close second has been Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But questions are now being raised by Republicans over whether a candidate not directly tied to the administration would be stronger. “Tuesday made clear that the stink on Vice President Vance and Secretary [Marco] Rubio may be too much to overcome as the election was a referendum on the job they are doing,” said one top GOP operative who has spoken to DeSantis. “This certainly creates a lane for DeSantis, Cruz and others if they are willing to run in a potentially impossible year to win,” the operative added. In blaming the losses on Iran, Vance put some daylight between himself and his boss. Trump, for his part, has doubled down in insisting his administration made the right decision to start the war. “Vance’s profile as a candidate is directly tied to the Trump legacy. A candidate for 2028 without an ability to craft a more unique, independent profile of their own will face challenges in this next two-year cycle,” Madden predicted. The GOP operative who spoke to The Hill said 2028 “is going to be a difficult year for Republican presidential contenders if there aren’t substantial changes.” If there aren’t changes, the operative said DeSantis might wait until 2032 to run for president. DeSantis over the last 48 hours or so has certainly sounded like someone with the White House on his mind. The Florida governor, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, was among the first this week to offer his own pointed view on what went wrong for GOP candidates, pointing to the war in Iran and high gas prices. In an interview with SiriusXM host Stephen A. Smith, he accused some in his party of “gaslighting” voters by not acknowledging their economic anxiety. DeSantis has also pointed out that the red wall in Florida, where the GOP won a Senate race and a gubernatorial contest, held. That’s an argument that would seem to point toward his leadership of the state. Republicans did lose three House races in districts that were redrawn to give GOP candidates an edge, and they are behind in a fourth. The gubernatorial and Senate races were also closer than expected. But DeSantis can certainly make an argument about his state being a GOP bastion. Cruz ahead of the elections had been more transparent about his ambition to run for president, saying he would entertain the idea of a 2028 run after the midterms. On his podcast, Cruz compared the losses to the drubbing Republicans took after Watergate, a comparison that would seem to at least raise the issue of corruption as being a factor in the GOP’s terrible night. He also criticized the Trump tariffs and the Iran war for raising costs. “Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high,” he said. GOP strategists predict that after Tuesday’s results, their primary will be wide open. “Vance is completely unacceptable to any Republican who can accurately assess the reasons for the pasting we received on Tuesday,” one former Trump campaign aide said. “It not only opens the door for others, it should soundly shut the door for JD Vance.” Other Republicans say Tuesday’s results force Vance to stake his claim early or face the consequences of a more crowded field. “Vance needs to announce first with the president’s endorsement,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “If he doesn’t do it in January, it’ll look like a sign of weakness and everyone will know the president isn’t on board. And that’s the million dollar question: Is he out of favor with the president?” One former Trump aide — who asked for anonymity to offer a candid assessment — said that right now, there’s “more space than less space” for other Republicans to enter the race. “Let’s face it, Cruz and DeSantis were the winners in our party the other night,” the former aide said. “This is absolutely the beginning of the end of the Trump era." The former aide added that Trump “is still going to be a potent force in the primary. If he endorses you, that’s 30 percent right off the bat." But the former aide predicted it would be difficult for Vance to keep his distance from Trump and that he would be pigeonholed to his stances. “Imagine, he’s going to have to answer to Trump’s whim or rant of the day every day,” the former aide said. “And he’s not going to stand in stark contrast to the president because Trump will shred him. “That’s just not an enviable place,” the former aide added. Since the elections, Vance has been under scrutiny from both Republicans and Democrats. Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer, who served under former President George W. Bush, took to social platform X to counter Vance’s evaluation of the sweeping GOP losses. “Please allow me to present a different perspective,” Fleischer said. “The problem was not the Iran War. It was the cease fire. If you start a war, you need to win it and finish it - otherwise don’t start it.” Democrats also pounced on Vance’s remarks. “For you to reduce it to a simple political calculation while we still have 50,000 troops in the Middle East, is one of the most crass, cynical things I’ve seen,” Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), wrote Wednesday on X. “You and President Trump got us into this war without a clear objective and without regard for the will of the American people. It’s cost us American lives and billions of dollars of American treasure with no end in sight.” On Thursday, as political pundits were saying it was the end of the Trump era, Republicans said Vance’s political future remained murky at best. “I think if you’re Vance you gotta take the nomination and pray you get someone on the other side like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez,” the first former Trump aide said, referring to the progressive representative from New York. For now, Del Percio said, results aside, Vance “ultimately stands in the same place he did three weeks ago.” “He only exists at the whim of the president,” she said. “And if Trump doesn’t endorse, will Vance go without the president’s endorsement? If he’s forced to do that, he will break with Trump and it will get ugly.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: Kenyan cult leader who ordered followers to starve children to death is jailed for 200 years
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Paul Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", the judge said last month [EPA] A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children. Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus". Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity. "The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added. The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention. The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation. The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years. Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies. Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment. However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration. "Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987. Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves. They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years. Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves. Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest". Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court. Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die. More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest [AFP via Getty Images] Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month. Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death. One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows". Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said. The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting. Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries. The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated. The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long. The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional. Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities. "We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023. Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings. "It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson." The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence. Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya. The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi. His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil". The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest. More about Kenya's doomsday cult from the BBC: 'My wife and six children joined Kenya starvation cult' What did the Kenyan starvation cult leader preach? The mother who fled a death cult to save her children [BBC] Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent. item.title: U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October as 'blowout' report trounces expectations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The US added 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past economists' expectations, as the labor market showed strength despite the Federal Reserve's recent rate hikes. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% even amid a slight increase in labor force participation. September's underwhelming jobs report of 29,000 additions was also revised upward to a gain of 60,000 jobs. Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, deemed the results "a blowout" in a post on X . Economists surveyed by Bloomberg projected a gain of about 70,000 jobs in October and saw the unemployment rate holding steady. Wage growth increased 0.4% from September, better than expectations for 0.3% month-over-month growth. Annual earnings rose 3.1%, beating expectations but likely still below the current inflation rate. Employers added jobs in a number of sectors of the economy. Professional and business services, which had been seen as more vulnerable to AI-related disruptions, added 70,000 roles. Healthcare, long a strong spot for job growth, added a higher-than-average 42,000 positions. Transportation and warehousing jobs rose by 25,000, and manufacturing continued to show strength with 19,000 additions. "This is still a low-hire, low-fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side," Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. Other job market measures released earlier this week telegraphed steady hiring — though not to the extent of Friday's report blowout number. Job openings and hiring edged higher , the Labor Department's monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey showed; private employers added 86,000 jobs , according to ADP; and layoff plans dropped to a three-year low while seasonal hiring ramped up. "Consistent with prior, more partial indicators of the US labor market, the October Jobs Report came in very strong, across the board," Wharton economist Mohamed El-Erian posted on X. The solid report will likely give the Federal Reserve more confidence to move forward with another rate hike in December . The central bank will also consider November jobs data and October's inflation figures before its Dec. 9 rate decision. Traders currently see a 77% chance of a 25 basis point rate hike next month, up from 67% on Thursday, according to CME FedWatch. "Today's jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions." Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/a-blowout-us-added-165000-jobs-in-october-trouncing-expectations-135651705.html

item.title: Trump doubles down on data centers amid market turmoil and voter backlash
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump reacted to the volatile Thursday in markets with a series of Truth Social posts overnight, doubling down on his support of data centers and trying to blame Democrats for the sell-off. A little after 7 a.m. ET Friday, he renewed his support for data centers , writing he "will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them" and calling leaders who might be opposed "foolish." The comments appeared largely directed at Texas, where voters this week elected a new Democratic governor who has promised to halt new data center construction in a race that surfaced deep voter unease over AI and its effects. President Donald Trump prominently displays a hat emblazoned with "Veto" in the Oval Office of the White House on November 5 after Democrats took control of the US House and Senate. (MANDEL NGAN / AFP via Getty Images) MANDEL NGAN via Getty Images Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa pledged on Thursday to protect Texas from data centers via new laws and, in the meantime, would hold off on approving new data center projects "until we have those protections." Hinojosa defeated outgoing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, one of the few losing figures Trump has lashed out at this week. Trump hasn't criticized most losing Republicans but reacted immediately to Abbott's loss , saying the three-term Republican governor would have won if he hadn't become a "RINO" (Republican in name only). "It wasn't pretty!" Trump boasted. The wave of anti-data center sentiment stretched across the country, elevating Democrats to governorships in places like Ohio and Georgia who could bring a newly critical eye to the sector in the middle of a rapid build-out. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa speaks at a press conference in Austin on November 5. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images) RONALDO SCHEMIDT via Getty Images The concerns about a slowdown in data center construction and AI spending led to a steep sell-off in tech stocks on Thursday — ending the worst post-midterm day since 1896 . Trump tried to pin blame for those losses on Democrats. "The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" Trump posted Thursday night on Truth Social . A day earlier, he was touting Wednesday's market gains , which came after the Democrats' sweeping win became clear. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. item.title: Brand faces 'significant' prison sentence after rape and sexual assault conviction
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Comedian Russell Brand at Southwark Crown Court in London. Anadolu via Getty Images Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison term after his rape and sexual assault conviction, a judge has said. A jury in London found the British comedian and actor guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault Thursday. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault. The judge told Brand he would be remanded in custody ahead of sentencing on Monday, Nov. 9. "You've been convicted of a number of offenses including rape," judge Joel Bennathan said. "The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I therefore have to remand you into custody." The actor had been charged on seven counts: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of attempted indecent assault. Following Thursday's verdict, London's Metropolitan Police Service told Yahoo News that Brand, 51, was facing further allegations of rape from two women. "The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations," the force said. Brand has not been charged in relation to these claims. The head of the Met Police, Sir Mark Rowley, has urged any other victims of Brand to contact the police. "There's two more rape allegations that we're looking at. We're encouraging anybody else to come forward if there's any other allegations," he told British media on Friday. He later said that he "wouldn't be surprised if many, many more come forward," adding of the trial, "This shows that powerful people can be brought down so you are safe stepping forward and we will support and try and bring that person to justice." Brand became a household name in the U.K. in the 2000s as a comedian and broadcaster. He went on to star in the movies Get Him to the Greek in 2010 and Arthur the following year. He married singer Katy Perry in October 2010, but Brand filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences. Their divorce was finalized in July 2012. The claims against Brand were made by six different women, spanning from 1999 to 2009. None of the women knew each other, but all of them came forward to police following a TV documentary and press reports in 2023, in which anonymous allegations were made by other women. Russell Brand was accompanied by his wife, Laura, during the trial. Neil Mockford via Getty Images During the trial, the court heard tearful and forceful testimony from the six complainants, who are all entitled to lifelong anonymity. The convictions included a rape that took place in 2009, involving a victim who went to Brand's home after meeting him at one of his shows. She said she had engaged in consensual sex, but that Brand then raped her and removed a condom in the process. Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman when he grabbed her breasts at a London bar in 2004. He was also found guilty over an incident in 2009, in which he demanded a woman give him a massage in front of two of his colleagues and then put his head in her groin. A third complaint of sexual assault ended in a guilty verdict when Brand was found guilty of pushing a woman who worked at a radio station up against a wall and forcibly kissing her. Brand denied the charges and said he had never forced anyone to do something against their will. CCTV footage released by the Met Police after the verdict shows Brand being interviewed by police in custody in December 2023. "As I've repeatedly stated publicly and written about extensively, I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I've spent years openly denouncing," Brand can be seen saying. "I've never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity." He said he did "not recall the names" of the complainants, or meeting them, adding, "However, it's entirely possible that I may have encountered them and we may have engaged in consensual sexual activity or physical contact that's been since reimagined." Following the verdict, the judge told Brand he would be remanded in custody. In a statement, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Met Police, said: "Today's verdict is first and foremost a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them." The statement added: "Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be." Ron Brand, Russell's father, told the BBC he was "shocked" by the verdicts. "I just didn't expect this — it's wrong," he said. "It's devastating." item.title: Hegseth strikes defiant tone in face of impeachment threat
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday dismissed a renewed effort in the House to bring articles of impeachment against him as early as next week. In a video on social media , Hegseth said, “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.” Hegseth was referring to Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who said Wednesday that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment when the House is back in session. Lawmakers are scheduled to return to Washington on Monday. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth added. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.” In the more-than-five-minute video, Hegseth only briefly touched on the Iran war — a driving force behind the effort to impeach him, as well as GOP losses in this week’s midterm elections. Massie, who lost his GOP primary after he crossed Trump, urged Trump on Thursday to replace Hegseth while he still has a GOP majority in the Senate. “My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials,” he said on X . “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns,” Massie wrote Wednesday . Numerous Democrats have indicated a desire to oust Hegseth since their midterm election wins, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York , who is poised to be the next speaker. Trump said Wednesday that he is not planning to replace Hegseth, and he said Thursday that Hegseth “has done a fantastic job” and “probably has opposition” over the actions he has taken, including purging military leadership. Trump has told some allies he is considering replacing Hegseth, asking them who they think should succeed him, two people familiar with discussions told NBC News this week. He has previously insisted that he was not considering dismissing department heads just days before they were shown the door. Massie tried to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth in September, but his efforts were stunted when House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., sent the House home early. He would need several Republicans to join all Democrats in supporting the impeachment measure for it to succeed. The House has impeached only two Cabinet officials in history — former President Joe Biden’s homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, in a partisan vote, and William Belknap, the secretary of war in the 1870s. No Cabinet members have ever been convicted by the Senate. item.description:

Democrats continue to celebrate one of the most lopsided midterm election victories in modern U.S. history, routing their Republican rivals to gain control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country. In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats and now hold 54 to the Republican Party's 44. Two seats — nail-biting contests in Alaska and Mississippi — remain undeclared. In the House, Democrats held 253 House seats to the GOP's 157 as of 10 a.m. ET Friday, comfortably passing the majority threshold of 218, with 25 races still to be called. The latest estimates show that the party is on track to win its largest majority since 2008. And there are still seats it could flip, including Colorado's Fourth District, which is held by Republican incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert, a staunch Trump ally, whose race against Democrat Eileen Laubacher remains tight. There were also 36 gubernatorial races , mayoral contests and numerous ballot measures — and plenty of firsts. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history, while Democrat Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor-elect. El-Sayed will be America's first Muslim senator. At the White House, President Trump signaled he would work with Democrats during his remaining two years in office but said he wouldn't hesitate to use his veto power. The president also acknowledged that the Iran war contributed to Republican losses, but defended his decision to pursue the conflict. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said, adding: "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon." Vice President JD Vance, though, blamed the scale of GOP losses squarely on the war with Iran. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," he wrote in a post on X . item.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production after years of poor sales
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Ananya Palyekar, Akanksha Khushi and Nick Carey Nov 6 (Reuters) - Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy ‌pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design. Musk said in an X ‌post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions. While it was not ​immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components. In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era". Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. ‌According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks ⁠in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units. "It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former ⁠Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same." "It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves." 'CYBERTRUCK WON'T GO, CAN'T GO' Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and ​safety ​experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like ​Europe. The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to ‌prove with a sledgehammer that its windows were shatterproof - only to leave massive cracks in two of them. During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future". But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations. Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market. "All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said. But Cybertruck's ‌sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory ​approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact. "Anywhere where you have ​crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't ​go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said. MUSK'S NEW BET The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, ‌pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in ​his push to turn Tesla into an ​AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker. Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis. After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. ​However, the automaker still has to answer the US ‌auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. "Cybertruck was an ​incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X. (Reporting by Ananya Palyekar and ​Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru; Editing by Jochelle Mendonca, Janane Venkatraman and Raju Gopalakrishnan) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/tesla-wind-down-cybertruck-production-094210977.html

item.title: Desert icons collapse as southwestern U.S. gets pummeled with rain and flooding
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
There are stretches of high desert in northwestern New Mexico where Mother Nature has sculpted otherworldly forms using wind, rain and the passage of time. Hefty planks of rock defy gravity as they balance atop spindly pedestals of clay, while some columns of sandstone take on the appearance of lace, elaborately eroded by the seasons. Tour guide Kialo Winters shares this piece of his homeland on the edge of the Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness with visitors regularly. On a recent Friday afternoon, the founder of Navajo Tours USA rounded a bend and found one of the area's most famous features had collapsed. The Alien Throne — or Tsé Bináká Níyol as it's known in his language — was no more. His heart dropped. “It was surreal,” he told The Associated Press. “I had to sort of just pause. A lot of things ran through my head.” The Alien Throne and the nearby King of Wings formation collapsed within weeks of each other, toppled by the very forces of nature that created them. Back-to-back storms destroy homes and hoodoos The southwestern U.S. has endured major rounds of storms over recent weeks, with rain falling on ground already soaked from an especially wet fall. Parts of New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona have watched rivers crest and floodwaters course through usually dry washes, destroying homes, further saturating the soil and eroding the landscape. The water is receding and cleanup is underway, but officials estimate the damage could stretch into the hundreds of millions of dollars. Winters still is concerned for relatives on the Navajo Nation, where many dirt roads became impassable or were washed away altogether by what he described as a series of massive storm fronts. Experts have estimated that more than 20 trillion gallons (75.7 trillion liters) of rain fell across the Four Corners states and Nevada during late October and early November as tropical moisture was funneled into the region. Condolences shared after the features collapse In early October, the demise of the King of Wings began circulating on social media. Visitors documented the large slab of rock on the ground near the mound of clay on which it once stood. It's not entirely clear when the Alien Throne came down, as poor road conditions kept Winters from visiting for a couple weeks. He had not seen any other posts about the feature's status until he rounded that corner Oct. 30 and saw it in pieces. Social media posts ranged from those who were thankful they were able to see the formations and immortalize them with photographs to those lamenting that they never had the chance. Condolences also were sprinkled in with debates about physics and the fragility of natural wonders. “Gravity. It’s not just a good idea … it’s the law,” one joked. These waypoints won't be forgotten For Winters and other Native Americans from the region, they’re more than just rock formations. They have served as waypoints, guiding ancestors along trade routes for thousands of years, and as connecting threads in stories handed down through generations. “They are culturally relevant to our identity and our stories,” he said, adding that their legacies will be carried on through photographs, illustrations and in the stories people share about their time spent in this stretch of desert. He called on people to let the sites “rest.” So no climbing on what remains, and certainly don't take any pieces home. It's far off the beaten path down a rutted, washboard dirt road. But it's worth it, said Alan Studt of Parma, Ohio, who made his first visit in 2019 and then again last April as part of a 50-day road trip. In looking back through his earlier photographs, he could see the formations were weathering. There were new holes forming in the throne and cracks along the wing's base, making it no surprise they would not last forever. Studt spent hours exploring and photographing the hills and washes during this last trip. He described being drawn in each time he saw a new set of spires in the distance, marveling at the petrified wood along the way and the rainbow of colors in the soils. “It is really so magical to be out there,” he said.
